text: In South Korea, the government says that having one child earns you two million won — about forty million Vietnamese dong.

Hungary goes even further, granting women with four or more children a lifetime exemption from personal income tax. Japan has even created an entire agency dedicated to caring for children and families.
Yet in all these countries, the birth rate keeps declining. I kept reading these statistics and wondering: why do people still refuse to have children, even with money?
The normal logic says they're probably too poor to have children. But now that they have money, shouldn't they have more? People used to have many children even when they were poor.
To explain this, we have to go back to the very first step of starting a family: dating. And we'll use the framework of game theory to explain why dating is becoming so difficult.
Why are there so many dating apps, yet so many people are still single? And with this trend of no one marrying or having children, many countries could disappear within a hundred years.
Welcome to our cat-themed adaptation series, where we adapt great foreign videos for you to learn from. We've always done this, but now we're making it official.

Our first series is the game theory series from the Predictive History channel. We'll base our content on those videos, plus our own research and counter-arguments, so we can all have better dinner-table conversations.
Okay, let's begin. First, a little about game theory. Any game has three parts: the players, who are the participants; the rules, the constraints on what can and can't be done; and the rewards.
Because there must be rewards in a game; no one plays for no reason. It's what makes players want to play.
To understand a game, we need to understand who is playing, what the rules are, and what the rewards are. Once we understand those three things, we can guess where the game is heading.
Okay, now let's apply this framework to dating. Imagine a society of ten people — five men and five women — and all of them want to date and get married.
These five men belong to five different social classes, ranked one to five based on appearance, health, wealth, and social status.
Number five will be the ultimate catch, while number one is the lowest. Instinctively, every woman wants to marry number five, and every man wants to marry all five women at once.

That's because women want a partner capable of protecting and providing for them, while men want to maximize their chances of having children, so they want to date many women at once. But if all the women only chase number five, it won't work.

Because the other four men will team up against number five. If number five tries to date all five women at once, everyone realizes he's not the most desirable choice after all — too promiscuous, with no guarantee of a future.
So the best option left for woman number five becomes man number four. That means woman number four loses her best option too, so she settles for man number three.
Then woman number three has to settle for man number two, and woman number two ends up with man number one. The result: man number five, the most eager one, ends up stuck with woman number one.
Technically woman number three could still end up with man number five, since the gap between five and two is large — but to keep things simple, let's assume the pattern above.

The final result: man number five, who should have won the best outcome, ends up with the worst one. Every woman ends up worse off too, except for woman number one. The only ones who benefit are the men — all of them.
This is just a small illustration, but it shows something important: in a game, the strongest player who gets too greedy ends up suffering, and their rivals become the ones who benefit directly.
From this we can deduce that the strongest person isn't the one who steals everything from everyone else — it's the one who can coordinate so everyone benefits the most.

Because if you just steal, you might win in the short term, but everyone loses in the long run. Even if man number four gets woman number five, there's still a gap between them, so conflict and difficulty are inevitable.
So the best solution is cooperation: man five takes woman five, man four takes woman four, man three takes woman three — everyone finds a partner, everyone has children, and society develops.

This state, in game theory, is called Nash equilibrium — a state where no one benefits from unilaterally changing their strategy. It's like everyone is happy, and any change would only cause more losses.
So we just keep things as they are. That theory works perfectly fine. But there's a problem: society doesn't have just ten people. It has eight billion.

Here's a fun survey question: if you're thirty years old, your parents are pressuring you to marry, you've been dating for ten years without finding anyone you like, and now you're forced to get married — what's the minimum you'd require to say yes?

For guys, it's simple: almost any woman would do, even woman number one. But some women say if they don't love the guy or find him attractive, he'd at least need to earn around two hundred million a month.

According to Nash equilibrium, woman number three should marry man number three and live happily. But in reality, she looks at him and thinks: better to stay single, unless I meet a number five, or someone earning two hundred million a month.
Because why suffer being with someone equal to you, risking having to constantly cater to him?

In reality, many people rush toward the top one or two percent, and most end up left behind. Elon Musk, for example, has a huge number of children and multiple wives — billionaires and celebrities never lack people lining up for them.
Meanwhile, many young people around the world experience involuntary singlehood — they want a partner, they want to marry, but they simply can't.

So gradually, they give up. Many guys would rather stay home playing games, browsing the internet, watching movies. Many young men in their twenties and thirties have never dated, never had a relationship, and don't want to try anymore.
It's not because they're ugly or incompetent — the dating game today is simply exhausting. Competition is fierce, and the odds of winning are low.
So the theory says balance is optimal, but in reality people don't want to play the game anymore. Why? Remember, a game has three parts. The players haven't changed much.
The rules — competition — haven't changed much either.

The final piece is the reward. Dating rewards used to mean love, sex, marriage, and children. But now there's another element that's become hugely exaggerated: social status — your reputation, your standing in the eyes of others.
Simply put: if you love and marry this person, can you show them off? Can you be proud in front of others?
Can you show them off on Facebook, on Instagram, at a class reunion — bragging about how handsome and rich your husband is, or how gorgeous and capable your wife is?

Reputation doesn't stop at marriage. It shows up in the latest iPhone, luxury travel check-ins, designer goods. Many people do these things not to use them, but to show off — and marriage has become part of that same game.
If you marry someone who isn't 'worthy,' it's embarrassing. So it's better to stay single than marry someone who doesn't meet the standard.

The scary part: this showing-off game is a zero-sum game. There will always be winners and losers. If everyone could show off, no one could show off — for there to be people at the top, there must be people at the bottom.
Many argue that government cash incentives for having children don't work, because the real problem isn't money. Finding a job today is easier than in the past, when people only knew how to farm.
Now people have more choices — they can get a normal job, stay healthy, and earn enough to live on. But what they lack is face — and face can't always be bought with money.
If you gave someone a billion dong to force them to marry someone their friends look down on, what would that billion even mean? It has some meaning, but ultimately...

...some people would rather skip a billion dong than have to marry beneath their status. So why do humans chase this 'face' when our species has survived tens of thousands of years without going extinct?
According to Mr. Giang from the Predictive History channel, humans didn't always behave this way — because the game itself changes over time.

Game theory has a concept called the overall context of society — the population size, whether society is rich or poor, whether there are external enemies, how advanced the technology is. These factors combine to determine which game gets played. When the context changes, the game changes too.
Let's divide human history into three stages. First: the primitive era. A small village back then had only about two hundred people, and everything was inconvenient and scarce.

People had to relieve themselves in the fields, sometimes getting bitten by snakes, and clean water had to be carried home and boiled before drinking. Having children in those conditions was like stepping into a death trap.

In that context there was no concept of love or dating. Men and women had many partners at once — partly to increase the odds of reproduction for everyone, partly so no one knew exactly whose child was whose.
When every man in the village thought a child might be his, everyone would protect and care for it together. The reward was simple: making sure the whole village didn't go extinct.
The second stage: the small village grows into a society of tens of thousands. Now there's money flowing in and out, and some early technology.
Villages, communes, and tribes start fighting each other constantly over territory and resources, so society becomes desperately short on people —
because it needs soldiers for war and hands to work the fields. In that kind of chaos, who has time for courtship and romance?

So arranged marriage takes center stage. Parents decide who their children marry, with no room for argument. Whether the couple likes each other doesn't matter — as long as they marry and have many children.
And finally, the third stage: today. The world is crowded — eight billion people. China and India alone each have over a billion.
There's much more money too, but wildly unequal — some have more than enough while others struggle to survive.
The upside: healthcare is better, technology more advanced, so women who give birth are almost guaranteed to survive — childbirth is no longer basically a death sentence.
And the world is relatively peaceful, in its own way — the superpowers no longer shoot each other directly, they wage proxy wars instead, or just talk tough.
Because life is better, people expect dating to be good too. And like everything else, dating, falling in love, and marriage come with both good and bad sides.

So if you have to endure hardship anyway, why date someone from your own social class and suffer together? Why not aim for someone from a higher class instead? Now dating works like a launching platform.
Lower-tier people try to climb to higher levels. Apps like Tinder, Bumble, or Facebook Dating are essentially platforms for finding a better match to jump to.

But if everyone wants to jump up a level, who's left to marry someone at their own level? It's like being a three but wanting a five, or at least a four — because if you're 'just' a three, why not stay put?
So marriage and birth rates are plummeting. Mr. Giang says if this trend continues, society will eventually collapse — and history has already proven it.

The clearest sign of a collapsing civilization is when women with money and education start refusing to have children. He's careful to say this isn't looking down on women — he loves women very much — but in part, the Roman Empire showed the same pattern when it fell.

When Rome was at its wealthiest and most skilled, the rich and capable decided not to have children, or to have very few. It got so serious that Emperor Augustus enacted the Lex Julia to punish those who avoided marriage and reward those with many children.

That means more than two thousand years ago, people already tried using money and policy to solve this problem — but the results weren't very effective. Rome collapsed anyway, though of course low birth rates were just one factor among many.

Let's look at the numbers. The replacement birth rate is 2.1 children per woman — the minimum for a population to stay stable. Below 2.1, we start losing people. Below 1.5, the decline is rapid. Below 1.0, a society is essentially self-destructing.

Looking at the world map: in Africa, birth rates are still very high — in some regions, five to seven children per mother — because those societies still need people to survive and compete for territory, so they compensate with more children.

Meanwhile in wealthy North America, Europe, and East Asia, birth rates are plummeting. North America and Europe still have immigration — if native-born women don't want children, immigrants fill the gap, working, paying taxes, contributing to the economy.

But that also causes real headaches around culture and politics — immigration is one of the hottest, most heated debates in Europe and America today. And East Asia is sitting on an outright powder keg.

East Asia has no such easy option, because East Asian culture is quite closed — it's hard to accept complete strangers at the same table. South Korea is the prime example: its birth rate has dropped to around 0.6 to 0.8, the lowest in the world.

At this rate, South Korea will likely survive only a few more generations before vanishing from the map. There are even restaurants there posting 'no kids allowed' signs — so-called no-kid zones — treating children as noisy nuisances that ruin the experience for other customers.

According to Mr. Giang, South Korea got this way because it's a society obsessed with appearances — everything has to be beautiful, high-quality, expensive. Just look at Korean showbiz: every idol and actor has to be flawlessly beautiful.

But where do idols and shows come from? Ordinary Koreans get caught in this same 'perfection trap,' and the path to success narrows sharply — either you get into a prestigious university and land a job at Samsung or a major corporation, or you have no decent options at all.

So a middle-class Korean family faces this brutal math: three children means needing more than three times the money and resources. If none of them can get into a top university, you might as well pour everything into just one child and send them to extra classes from dawn until night, hoping they'll pass and change the family's fortunes.

This logic pushes people to have only one child, or none at all, just to avoid the burden. Korea's population looks stable for now because there's still a large working-age group — but by around 2040 the imbalance kicks in: the elderly population will explode while the number of children keeps shrinking.

By 2060, the workforce could be cut in half. At that point, there's no one left to work, no one to serve in the military — a society of elderly people sitting in parks with no one creating wealth, headed straight for economic collapse. China faces the same story: its birth rate is now only about 1.0.
Just five years ago China's rate was still 1.7 — now it's collapsing fast. At this pace, by the end of the century China's population could be cut in half, down to around 600 million.

That's still a lot of people, but with so many elderly, the system won't be able to support them. Here's an interesting comparison though: usually the richer a country, the fewer children it has — but there are exceptions.

Israel is rich and highly advanced technologically, yet families there still average more than two children. Through the lens of game theory, the reward structure in Israel is different because of history and religion — having children is tied to community identity and national survival, something to be proud of, not a burden.

Or take an oil-rich nation like Saudi Arabia — people still have many children because oil wealth means the state provides everything: healthcare, housing, all free. Add religious factors that encourage large families, and people just keep having kids. Whether that model survives once the oil runs out is a question only the future can answer.

The key insight: from a game-theory view, societies where having children boosts your prestige will have high birth rates. Societies where having children diminishes your prestige — where it means losing freedom, money, time, and opportunities for advancement — people will simply choose not to have children.
So now the question is: what about Vietnam?
In 2024, Vietnam's birth rate fell to 1.91 per woman — the lowest in our history, and the third consecutive year below the replacement rate of 2.1. The downward trend is unmistakable.

Interestingly, 2024 was the Year of the Dragon — traditionally a very auspicious year to have children, and even the person writing this script was born in a Dragon year. But even strong spiritual beliefs can't beat the modern game of saving face.
Everyone knows the Dragon year is lucky, but once people weigh the expense, the exhaustion of raising kids, and the toll on their careers, they give up on having children anyway.

In big cities the birth rate is only 1.67; rural areas are slightly higher but still declining. Ho Chi Minh City has the lowest rate in the country at just 1.39, while the average age of first marriage keeps rising — men around thirty, women around twenty-five.

This fits the game-theory framework perfectly: the more educated and wealthier people are, the fewer children they have, because they have far more to lose. Many experts predict that after 2035, Vietnam's population growth could turn negative — deaths outnumbering births — and seven provinces may already be experiencing this.
Vietnam isn't as extreme as South Korea or China yet, but we're on the same path — and we're just as heavily shaped by social media.

In the old days, people lived in a small village or neighborhood of a few hundred people and only compared themselves to those around them. The odds of being the 'best' in the neighborhood were fairly high.
Even moving to Hanoi or Saigon and being just average, people were still happy to marry and raise their children with less comparison — and they were considered great for it.

Now it's completely different. On TikTok you see guys with six-pack abs driving Porsches, building fortunes. On Instagram, girls with flawless skin, slim waists, designer bags. Anyone successful becomes known to the whole society.
So naturally, you start comparing yourself to millions of people online — and suddenly the people actually around you don't seem good enough anymore.

Social media expanded the playing field from two or three hundred people to millions, pushing standards up unreasonably. Dating apps work the same way — swiping through hundreds of profiles a day tricks your brain into thinking you have unlimited choices.
There's no need to rush, you think — just keep swiping, better people are surely coming. The result: you end up choosing no one, or you don't even like the person once you do go on a date.

From a game-theory perspective, social media multiplied the number of players a thousandfold, while the number of prizes at the top stayed exactly the same — so the win rate is practically zero. But people keep playing anyway, simply because everyone else is playing.
After making this video, we realized game theory doesn't hand us an immediate answer — it only teaches us how to ask the right question: who are the players, what are the rules, what are the rewards?

From there you can see the bigger picture — where a society stands, and where it's heading. Dating is just one example; the same framework applies to everything, from US-Iran tensions to the war in Ukraine, to why this moment could be Vietnam's opportunity to break through.

Okay, that's enough for now. What do you think — is this game of saving face affecting your own dating and marriage decisions, or are there other factors at play? Let us know in the comments, and don't forget to subscribe so you don't miss the next video.
